items.title: 10.20 Activity series of metals and ease of oxidation

source_refs.note: Topic 10.20 with Table 10.2, printed pages 236-237. Table typos ('-.1.66', '-O.40') are corrected; the printed order Hg +0.92 above Ag +0.80 is kept.

blocks.title: Activity series
blocks.text: The activity series of metals is a ranking of metals by their reactivity, particularly their tendency to lose electrons and undergo oxidation. It is in fact a reactivity series.

Metals higher in the series have more negative standard reduction potentials, are more likely to lose electrons and be oxidised, and so act as reducing agents; metals at the top are the most reactive with water, oxygen and acid. Alkali metals such as caesium and sodium are highly reactive and oxidise readily, reacting vigorously with water to form ions and release hydrogen. Metals lower in the series, such as the noble metals gold and silver, do not oxidise easily; they are less reactive, do not readily lose electrons, and do not react with water. Metals at the bottom are the least reactive with water, oxygen and acid. Conversely, metals lower in the series have more positive standard reduction potentials, a greater tendency to gain electrons and be reduced, and so their ions act as oxidising agents. The position of a metal in the series correlates directly with its ease of oxidation and overall reactivity, as Table 10.2 shows.

blocks.long_description: The potential of a cell is not fixed: for copper reacting with silver ions it climbs in a straight line as the logarithm of the silver ion concentration rises, reaching the standard 0.46 V at unit concentration, which is what the Nernst equation describes, and for zinc in dilute zinc ions the potential drops below -0.76 V. Listing metals by their standard potentials gives the activity series, from lithium and the alkali metals that react with cold water, through magnesium reacting with steam and the metals that only displace hydrogen from acids, past hydrogen itself, to copper, silver, platinum and gold that resist both water and acids; a higher metal displaces a lower one from solution. Photovoltaic cells turn light into electricity through a PN junction. In a polluted river bacteria consuming organic matter raise the biochemical oxygen demand while the dissolved oxygen falls, the inverse relation measured by the Winkler iodine titration.
